### Introduction

This project examines the differences in educational development and opportunity around the world. The quality of education among a country's population is one of the most prominent indicators of the current wellbeing and future advancement of a country, yet it varies significantly across different places and groups of people. I was curious about the extent of these differences, so I turned to the data to find out.

I used data from the United Nations' Human Development Reports by the UN Development Program; I obtained data from [UNDP's open database](https://hdr.undp.org/data-center/documentation-and-downloads) which covers 34 years: 1990 to 2023. Note that the variables that I was interested in were missing data past 2023 so the past couple of years (2024 and 2025) aren't included in this analysis.

The data contains information on countries' adult population, defined as people over 25 for the metrics I'm interested in, and specifically their average amount of education that they've attained by then. There are also more variables providing breakdowns by demographics, such as the same metrics split by gender as well as indicators of the country's economic level of development in the form of the GNI (Gross National Income) of the residents, which provide extra quantitative context on a country. The dataset also includes global versions of these metrics.

```{r include = FALSE}
# Loading packages
library(readxl)
library(tidyverse)
library(countrycode)
library(scales)
library(gghighlight)
library(ggrepel)
library(gt)
library(gtExtras)
library(sf)
library(rnaturalearth)

# Preparing the data

populations <- countrypops %>%
  filter(year == 2023) %>%
  select(country_code_3, population)

data <- read_excel("hdr-data.xlsx") %>%
  select(-c(yearStr, indexCode, index, dimension, note)) %>%
  mutate((across(c(year, value, actualValue), as.numeric)),
         continent = countrycode(countryIsoCode,
                                 origin = "iso3c",
                                 destination = "continent"),
         # NRO is for Naoero, a country in Oceania
         # ZZK.WORLD means the global value
         continent = ifelse(countryIsoCode == "NRO", "Oceania", continent)) %>%
  # Joining the UN data with populations
  left_join(populations, by = c("countryIsoCode" = "country_code_3"))

# Checking the data

# TODO: check for missing values, duplicates, and outliers

```

### Viewing the global level of education over time

Just as a preliminary look, in this initial plot of the average amount of education worldwide in years, it's clear that the world is gradually becoming more educated as a whole.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
# Graphing the global education mean over time
data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys",
         is.na(continent)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = actualValue)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = ~ paste(.x, "Years"),
                     limits = c(NA, 9)) +
  labs(x = "", y = "",
       title = "Average Amount of Education That Adults* Have (1990-2023)",
       caption = "*Adults 25+") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(t = 0, r = 15, b = 0, l = 0)),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 14))

# Calculating the average change in MYS per year

mys_1990 <- data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys", is.na(continent), year == 1990) %>%
  pull(actualValue)

mys_2023 <- data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys", is.na(continent), year == 2023) %>%
  pull(actualValue)
```

The world's education level in general has been steadily growing for the past 3 decades from ~`r round(mys_1990, 1)` years in 1990 to ~`r round(mys_2023, 1)` years in 2023 (a change of ~`r round(mys_2023 - mys_1990, 1)` years!), which is really nice to see. In fact, it has increased every single year, by ~`r round((mys_2023 - mys_1990) / (2023 - 1990), 1)` years each year.

However, if we look into how the level of education varies demographically and geographically, some disparities emerge.

### Exploring differences by gender

In this plot, when the metric is split by gender, a gap emerges.

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
# Graphing the global education mean by gender over time
data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode %in% c("mys_f", "mys_m"),
         is.na(continent)) %>%
  mutate(indicatorCode = recode(indicatorCode,
                                "mys_f" = "Females",
                                "mys_m" = "Males")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = actualValue, colour = indicatorCode)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Males" = "royalblue2",
                                "Females" = "violetred1")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = ~ paste(.x, "Years")) +
  labs(x = "", y = "",
       title = "Average Amount of Education That Adults Have (1990-2023)",
       colour = "") +
  guides(color = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE)) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(t = 0, r = 15, b = 0, l = 0)),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 14),
        legend.position = c(0.1, 0.9))
```

The average amount of education for females has never been more than for males. Although they've been increasing at very similar speeds — the lines are nearly parallel — there has consistently been a gap of around a year between them. Nonetheless, over the past few years, beginning in 2020, that gap has been shrinking a little.

In this table, which includes every 5 years up to 2023 for conciseness, you can see the gender gap each year. In 2020, the magnitude of the gap dropped to a new low of 0.8 years.

```{r echo=FALSE}
# Putting the yearly gaps in a table
data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode %in% c("mys_f", "mys_m"), is.na(continent)) %>%
  group_by(year, indicatorCode) %>%
  summarize(actualValue = mean(actualValue, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = indicatorCode, values_from = actualValue, values_fill = 0) %>%
  mutate(gap = round(mys_m - mys_f, 1)) %>%
  filter(year %in% c(1990, 1995, 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2023)) %>%
  select(year, gap) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = gap) %>%
  # Styling the table
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(decimals = 1) %>%
  cols_align("center") %>%
  tab_header(title = "Gender Gaps in Education Over Time") %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(size = px(18)),
            locations = cells_title(groups = "title")) %>%
  tab_options(table.border.top.color = "white",
              column_labels.background.color = "grey95")
```

Another way to look at the gender gap is through the percentage of adults in each gender who have at least some level of secondary education, where secondary education, under the [UN's International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED)](https://www.uis.unesco.org/sites/default/files/medias/fichiers/2025/08/EDS-3-ISCED-Final-WEB.pdf), is defined as an intermediate phase of education spanning ages 11 to 18.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
# Graphing the percentage of people who have secondary education by gender over time
data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode %in% c("se_f", "se_m"),
         is.na(continent)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = actualValue, fill = indicatorCode)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("se_m" = "royalblue2", "se_f" = "violetred1"),
                    labels = c("se_m" = "Males", "se_f" = "Females")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(scale = 1),
                     limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(x = "",
       y = "",
       title = "Percentage of Adults With Secondary Education (1990-2023)",
       fill = "") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(t = 0, r = 15, b = 0, l = 0)),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 14),
        legend.position = c(0.1, 0.9)) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE))
```

Again, the percentage of females with education worldwide has never exceeded the percentage of males, with a consistent difference of ~10%, but this has shrunk to around 8.2% in 2023.

```{r echo=FALSE}
# Putting the yearly gaps in a table
data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode %in% c("se_f", "se_m"), is.na(continent)) %>%
  group_by(year, indicatorCode) %>%
  summarize(actualValue = mean(actualValue, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = indicatorCode, values_from = actualValue, values_fill = 0) %>%
  mutate(gap = se_m - se_f, 1) %>%
  filter(year %in% c(1990, 1995, 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2023)) %>%
  select(year, gap) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = gap) %>%
  # Styling the table
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(decimals = 1) %>%
  cols_align("center") %>%
  tab_header(title = "Gender Gaps in Education Over Time") %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(size = px(18)),
            locations = cells_title(groups = "title")) %>%
  tab_options(table.border.top.color = "white",
              column_labels.background.color = "grey95")
```

### Exploring differences by location

Below is a graph of each continent's average amount of education of its population who are over 25 years old.

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
# Graphing the global education mean by continent over time
data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys",
         !is.na(continent)) %>%
  group_by(continent, year) %>%
  summarise(mean_mys = mean(actualValue, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_mys, colour = continent)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "",
       y = "",
       title = "Average Amount of Education That Adults Have (1990-2023)",
       colour = "Continent") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = ~ paste(.x, "Years")) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(t = 0, r = 15, b = 0, l = 0)),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 14)) +
  scale_colour_brewer(type = "qual", palette = 6)
```

```{r echo=FALSE}
# Getting the countries with consistently high education rates
top_countries = data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys",
         !is.na(continent)) %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  # Ranking countries by the metric in ascending order
  mutate(rank = rank(actualValue, ties.method = "min")) %>%
  # Keeping only the top 10 for each year
  filter(rank >= 10) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  # Counting how many times each country appeared in the top 10
  count(continent, country, name = "times_in_top_10")
```


Additionally, here are the countries that have been in the bottom 10 at least once. There are 17 countries that have been in the bottom 10 at least once, of which 4 countries (Afghanistan, Guinea, Mali, and Niger) have been there in every year from 1990 to 2023.

```{r echo=FALSE}
# Making a table of the least educated countries (1990-2023)
bottom_countries = data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys") %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  mutate(rank = rank(actualValue, ties.method = "min")) %>%
  filter(rank <= 10) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  count(continent, country, name = "times_in_bottom_10")

# Making a table of the countries with consistently high education rates
bottom_countries %>%
  # Styling the table
  gt() %>%
  cols_align("center") %>%
  cols_label(continent = "Continent",
             country = "Country",
             times_in_bottom_10 = "# of Times in Bottom 10") %>%
  tab_header(title = "Countries With Consistently Low Education Rates (1990-2023)") %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(size = px(18)),
            locations = cells_title(groups = "title")) %>%
  tab_options(table.border.top.color = "white",
              column_labels.background.color = "grey95")
```

```{r echo=FALSE}
# Calculating the exact change between 1990 and 2023

changes <- data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys") %>%
  group_by(country) %>%

  summarise(earliest_year = min(year[!is.na(actualValue)]),
```

To illustrate the widest global gaps, here are the differences between the highest and lowest-ranked countries over the years.

```{r echo=FALSE}
# Putting the yearly gaps in a table
data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys", !is.na(continent)) %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(Highest = country[which.max(actualValue)],
            Lowest = country[which.min(actualValue)],
            Gap = round(max(actualValue, na.rm = TRUE) - min(actualValue, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  gt() %>%
  cols_align("center") %>%
  cols_label(year = "Year") %>%
  tab_header(title = "Gaps in Education Across Countries Over Time") %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(size = px(18)),
            locations = cells_title(groups = "title")) %>%
  tab_options(table.border.top.color = "white",
              column_labels.background.color = "grey95")
```

The gap has remained the same, mostly because the rate of growth has been similar around the world.

Here are the top 5 countries in 2023, again in terms of the average time spent in education of the portion of its population who are over 25.

```{r warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Making a table of the most educated countries in 2023
# TODO: change title
# TODO: change colors
data %>%
  filter(year == 2023, indicatorCode == "mys") %>%
  arrange(desc(actualValue)) %>%
  select(continent, country, actualValue, population) %>%
  head(n = 5) %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(decimals = 1) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = population,

  cols_align("center") %>%
  cols_label(continent = "Continent",

             actualValue = "Mean Years of Education",
```
